findings.title: OpenAI site tools (WebMCP) — any website can hand tools to a visiting ChatGPT or Codex agent, with no install, no config file, and tool definitions that OpenAI documents as untrusted
findings.description: On **August 25, 2026** OpenAI shipped **site tools**, its implementation of the proposed **WebMCP** standard, in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser and in ChatGPT Sites. A page registers a tool by calling **`document.modelContext.registerTool()`** in ordinary JavaScript, supplying a name, a description, an input schema, an **execute handler that calls the application's existing logic**, and annotations such as `readOnlyHint`. A compatible agent — **ChatGPT Work or Codex** — **discovers the available tools automatically when the page loads** and invokes the relevant ones while completing the user's task. **Every assumption behind existing tool inventory breaks here.** There is no installation event, so nothing is ever written to disk or to a settings file; there is no marketplace or registry, so there is no catalogue to enumerate; there is no server, so there is no endpoint to inspect out-of-band; and the tool set **exists only for the lifetime of the page**, which means an agent's capability set is now a function of navigation history rather than configuration. This is a different problem from the Agent Plugins/`mcp.json` gap reported on 08-24 — that was an artifact in the wrong file, this is **no artifact at all**. OpenAI's own documentation supplies the threat model in its own words: "**Website-provided tool definitions and results are untrusted content**", "**tool names alone don't prove function or scope**", "website instructions don't grant permission for unrelated actions", and, on its mitigations, "**these checks reduce risk; they don't make a website or its output trustworthy**." Three specifics make this actionable. **First, tools run inside the site's existing authenticated session** — the execute handler is the site's own code calling its own logic with the logged-in user's permissions, so a site tool's blast radius is exactly what the user can do on that site, reached without the user clicking anything. **Second, the mitigations are per-invocation and local**: each invocation gets a safety review, the browser ties invocations to the originating page, normal website-access and confirmation policies still apply for consequential actions (sending messages, purchases, deleting data, changing permissions), and users can inspect the tool list via a **"Site tools" button in the address bar** or disable the feature under **Settings > Browser > Permissions** — all of which are user-facing controls with no tenant-level policy surface documented. **Third, and most important for coverage: it is withheld from Enterprise and Edu workspaces**, and it requires **GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra** (Luna has it disabled). So the population that has it is Plus/Pro/Business on a personal or unmanaged-tier account — precisely the population an enterprise sees least. AIRT should treat a WebMCP-enabled page as a first-class injection and tool-abuse vector, and test the specific shape this creates: a tool whose *description* is adversarial (the model chooses tools by description, and the description is attacker-authored), a tool whose *name* implies a benign scope while its handler does something else (OpenAI names this failure explicitly), a `readOnlyHint` annotation that is simply false, and tool *results* used to steer subsequent turns. ENDPOINT must stop treating tool availability as static endpoint state: capability now arrives per-navigation, so the signal to collect is browsing-plus-invocation telemetry from the desktop app, not a file inventory. AISPM should model "site tool" as an ephemeral tool entity bound to an origin rather than to an agent or an install, and treat the **origin** as the provenance record it will never get from a manifest

findings.title: ChatGPT scheduled tasks can now be triggered by inbound Gmail, Slack and GitHub events — an outsider who can email the user can cause an authenticated agent to run
findings.description: Also on **August 25, 2026**, OpenAI made scheduled tasks event-driven. A task can now fire on **a new Gmail message** (optionally filtered by sender or subject), **a new message in a watched Slack channel**, or **pull-request activity in an authorized github.com repository** — including reviews, comments, commit updates and merges. The user connects the account under **Settings > Apps**, describes the event and the action in Work, then reviews a **Trigger, Condition and Prompt** triple and completes authorization. The **ChatGPT Slack app must be a member of every watched channel** and the **GitHub app needs repository access**, so the trigger carries its own standing integration grant. Time-based schedules and event triggers **cannot coexist** on a single task, and **clustered events may be combined into a single run**. Available on Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu, plus ChatGPT for Healthcare workspaces. **The security consequence is a change in who initiates agent activity.** Until now an agent run in ChatGPT was traceable to a human action — a prompt, or a schedule that a human set. An event trigger inverts this: **the initiating party is whoever authored the triggering content**, and for the three named sources that party is frequently external. Anyone who can send the user an email, post in a Slack channel the ChatGPT app has joined, or comment on a pull request in an authorized repo can now cause an authenticated agent run to happen, at a time of their choosing, on text they wrote. That is the classic indirect-prompt-injection precondition with the delivery problem solved for the attacker: they no longer need the user to paste anything or open anything. **The filters are the attack surface, not the control** — "filter by sender or subject" is attacker-observable and attacker-satisfiable, and a sender filter is only as strong as the absence of spoofing and forwarding. Two second-order properties matter for detection. **Event clustering** means one agent run may correspond to several triggering messages, so the mapping from external content to agent action is many-to-one and cannot be reconstructed from the run alone. And because triggers are configured per task with their own connected app, **the standing grant outlives the user's attention**: a task configured once keeps consuming external content indefinitely with no session for a human to be present in. AIDR should treat event-triggered task runs as a distinct activity type from user-initiated and schedule-initiated runs, capture the triggering source (Gmail sender/subject, Slack channel and author, GitHub repo/PR/actor) as first-class attribution, and alert on the shape that matters: an externally-triggered run that subsequently touches internal data or invokes a write-capable connector. AISPM should inventory event-triggered tasks as standing automations with an external trigger surface, record which apps each is bound to and which channels/repos are watched, and flag tasks whose trigger is broad (any new Gmail message, a high-traffic public channel, a repo with external contributors)

findings.title: AWS Agent Registry can now be shared across accounts via RAM, and three of the four managed permissions grant live MCP invocation — with automatic acceptance inside an Organization
findings.description: AWS added **cross-account sharing to the AWS Agent Registry** through **AWS Resource Access Manager**. The registry — the "private, governed catalog of agents, tools, skills, MCP servers, and custom resources" reported on 2026-08-07 — is now a shareable RAM resource type (`agent-registry:Registry`), and the owner selects one of four AWS managed permissions that RAM enforces through a resource-based policy it manages. **The permission tiers are the finding.** `AWSRAMDefaultPermissionAgentRegistryReadOnly` (the default when no permission is specified) grants control-plane reads plus data-plane discovery but **explicitly not** MCP invocation. `AWSRAMPermissionAgentRegistryForConsumer` grants discovery **plus `agent-registry:InvokeRegistryMcp`** — and AWS's own tip recommends it as the default choice: "We recommend the **Consumer** permission for typical sharing scenarios." `AWSRAMPermissionAgentRegistryForPublisher` adds `CreateRegistryRecord`, `UpdateRegistryRecord`, `DeleteRegistryRecord` and `SubmitRegistryRecordForApproval`. `AWSRAMPermissionAgentRegistryForAdmin` adds **`UpdateRegistryRecordStatus`** — approve, reject or deprecate records — so **curation authority over a registry can be delegated to a different AWS account** while `UpdateRegistry`/`DeleteRegistry` stay with the owner. Read together: the recommended sharing posture is not "let another account look at the catalogue", it is "**let another account's agents invoke tools through my registry's MCP endpoint**", and the most permissive tier lets a foreign account decide which records are approved for everyone. **The consent model is the second half.** For accounts outside the owner's Organization, RAM sends an invitation the consumer must accept. **For accounts inside the same Organization with RAM org-sharing enabled, acceptance is automatic — no invitation, no consumer-side action, no event for the consumer to notice.** So in the common enterprise case, a registry share simply appears, and any Zenity model that expects a two-sided handshake will miss it entirely. Revocation is likewise **eventually consistent, with up to ~30 seconds of continued access after `disassociate-resource-share`**. **Third, the fine-grained controls have a documented enumeration hole.** The two service condition keys — **`agent-registry:RecordCreatorAccount`** and **`agent-registry:RecordSourceAccount`** — are resolved at authorization time from the stored record and cannot be set from request input (good), but AWS states they are **not evaluated** on `CreateRegistryRecord`, nor on **`SearchDiscoverableRegistryRecords`, `ListRegistryRecords` or `ListDiscoverableRegistryRecords`**, which "return summaries for all matching records regardless of condition-key restrictions." AWS's own remediation is to withhold search and list from the share — which almost nobody will do, because discovery is the point. So a consumer scoped by condition key to its own records can still **enumerate the full catalogue of another account's agents, tools and MCP servers**. AISPM should treat a shared registry as a cross-account trust edge, not an attribute: discover RAM resource shares over `agent-registry:Registry`, resolve which managed (or customer-managed) permission each carries, and materially distinguish shares that include `InvokeRegistryMcp` from those that don't. Flag `ForAdmin` shares as delegated curation authority, flag org-internal shares as having no acceptance event, flag any customer-managed permission that grants list/search alongside condition keys as an enumeration exposure, and correlate registry records against the consumer accounts that can reach them so a "private, governed catalog" is not scored as single-account when it is not

findings.title: Microsoft Agent Hooks — a framework-neutral, fail-closed agent interception contract with eight named control points and three documented bypasses
findings.description: Microsoft Agent Framework has shipped **Agent Hooks**, described by Microsoft as "a first-class Agent Framework capability for applying governance and runtime controls at well-defined points in an agent's execution," and it implements **AGENT-HOOKS-0.1**, a **framework-neutral contract** published at `github.com/responsibleai/agent-hooks` so that "policy engines, approval gateways, budget guards, content filters, and egress controls can target one common control surface." It reached first-class experimental status in **.NET 1.19.0 on August 22** and is experimental in the Python SDK; the doc pages were refreshed **2026-08-25**. **Why this is a coverage item and not just a competitor feature:** Agent Hooks is where an enterprise's agent controls will increasingly live, so Zenity needs to inventory it, read its verdicts, and know exactly where its guarantees stop. **The control surface is eight named interception points** — `agent_startup`, `input`, `pre_model_call`, `post_model_call`, `pre_tool_call`, `post_tool_call`, `output`, `agent_shutdown` — each with a defined transform target (messages to the model, tool arguments, tool results, final response content). **The verdict vocabulary is five-valued**: `allow`, `warn`, `deny`, **`escalate`** (a liftable deny resolved through an approval channel), and `transform` (rewrite a value at a `$target` path). Microsoft states the runtime guarantees explicitly: **fail closed** — "invalid contexts, invalid verdicts, interceptor failures, and enforcement failures don't silently bypass controls"; **transform write-back**, where a transform that can't be applied fails the run; **buffered streaming**, where no update reaches the caller until the full response has passed `post_model_call` and `output`; **verdict-gated persistence**; and **complete bundle installation**, so "an incomplete enforcement boundary can't be configured accidentally." **The three bypasses Microsoft documents are the highest-value part of this finding, because each is a place where a customer will believe they are protected and not be.** (1) **Provider-executed hosted tools do not pass through the function-invocation seam at all** — their calls and outputs surface at `post_model_call`, but `pre_tool_call` and `post_tool_call` "can't block the provider's server-side execution." An agent whose tools are hosted by the model provider therefore has *no* enforceable tool gate, only after-the-fact visibility. (2) **Middleware registered before the bundle is outside the boundary** — "treat outer position as outer trust" — so ordering, not presence, determines coverage, and a misordered stack silently reduces the enforcement surface. (3) **The contract is "cooperative rather than a process isolation boundary"**: interceptors run in the host process, receive the full content, and are not sandboxed — "only register interceptors you trust", and "code paths that bypass the guarded agent pipeline aren't covered." A fourth, subtler gap sits in persistence: with `require_per_service_call_history_persistence=True`, each model exchange is persisted once its `post_model_call` verdict permits it, and **"a later `output` deny doesn't roll back that already permitted history"** — so an output-only egress policy leaves model content durable. **And the mode flag is a posture attribute in its own right**: `evaluate_only` runs every interceptor and records every verdict while **allowing every action**, with Microsoft warning "don't describe an `evaluate_only` deployment as enforced governance." An agent with hooks installed in `evaluate_only` looks governed and is not — exactly the kind of false-assurance state AISPM exists to surface. Note also the availability asymmetry: **Python only**; .NET and Go agents are directed to plain middleware, tool approval and Agent Safety instead, so within one customer's fleet the same nominal control exists on some agents and not others. AISPM should discover which Agent Framework agents have an Agent Hooks bundle installed, record the **mode** (`enforce` vs `evaluate_only`), the **composition** profile (default is sequential `first_deny`), whether a `resolver` is configured (without one, every `escalate` is simply a deny), the interceptor set and its **order relative to other middleware**, and whether the agent uses provider-hosted tools — because that last fact converts a nominally complete boundary into an incomplete one. The **`record_sink` `InterceptionRecord` stream** is a first-class ingestion target for AIDR: it carries decision, reason, interceptor summary, mode, identity and sequence, deliberately **without the intercepted payload**, which makes it high-signal and low-sensitivity — but also means Zenity cannot reconstruct *what* was blocked from the record alone

findings.title: Microsoft FIDES — deterministic information-flow control with trust and confidentiality labels on agent content, shipping in Agent Framework and never reported by this monitor
findings.description: **FIDES** (Flow Integrity Deterministic Enforcement System) is information-flow control as first-class middleware in Microsoft Agent Framework, based on the [FIDES paper by Costa et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23643), shipping in `agent-framework-core` behind `agent_framework.security` as an experimental feature. It has been documented since **ms.date 2026-06-23** — this is a **two-month coverage gap**, surfaced only because the page was refreshed **2026-08-25**. Microsoft's framing is a direct attack on the heuristics Zenity's customers currently rely on: defensive system prompts and hand-rolled allow-lists "are heuristic… they don't make the next attack impossible," sanitization "is lossy," and "pre/post-hoc monitoring detects damage; it doesn't prevent it." **The mechanism is a two-axis label on every piece of content.** **Integrity** is `trusted` (developer-controlled: system prompt, internal database, signed config) or `untrusted` ("anything the model could have been tricked into ingesting — issue bodies, emails, scraped pages, third-party API responses"). **Confidentiality** is `public`, `private`, or `user_identity` (PII, credentials, per-user secrets). Labels combine **most-restrictive-wins** (`untrusted` beats `trusted`; `user_identity` > `private` > `public`) and propagate automatically through tool calls via `LabelTrackingFunctionMiddleware`. **Sinks declare what context they will run in**, and these two annotations are the enforcement primitive worth internalizing: **`accepts_untrusted: False`** refuses a tool outright when anything untrusted is in scope (intended for "file writes, destructive operations, anything that mutates production state"), and **`max_allowed_confidentiality`** caps what a sink may leak (`public` for anything that publishes externally). `PolicyEnforcementFunctionMiddleware` checks each invocation **before the tool runs**. There is also a strong-isolation mode: with **`auto_hide_untrusted=True` (the default)**, untrusted tool results never reach the main model at all — they are stashed in a `ContentVariableStore` and replaced in context by a **`var_<id>` reference**, and the agent must call **`quarantined_llm`** to process them, which dispatches an isolated completion against a separate chat client **with no tools attached** and labels its own output untrusted. **Three things make this directly actionable for Zenity.** **First, it is a ready-made vocabulary for findings Zenity already produces.** "Untrusted content reached a privileged sink" and "private content reached a public sink" are now *named, vendor-documented* conditions with a deterministic definition, on a Microsoft-supported runtime. Zenity's own toxic-combination model should adopt this framing — an agent whose reachable tool set contains a sink with no `accepts_untrusted` declaration, or whose `max_allowed_confidentiality` cap is looser than its data sources, is a computable posture defect rather than a judgement call. **Second, its configuration surface is a posture surface with real false-assurance states.** `enable_policy_enforcement=False` is the documented **dry-run mode**: labels still propagate, the audit log still fills, and **no sink is ever blocked** — an agent in this state produces governance telemetry while enforcing nothing. `approval_on_violation=True` converts blocks into human approval prompts, which means the control's effectiveness collapses to user click-through behaviour. `allow_untrusted_tools` is an explicit per-tool exemption list. And **`default_integrity` can be flipped from the secure-by-default `UNTRUSTED` to `TRUSTED`**, which silently relabels every unannotated tool's output as safe. Each of these is a discoverable configuration Zenity should read and score. **Third, its documented limitations are a coverage map.** Labels are **opt-in per data source** — "a tool you forget to label" falls back to defaults; propagation is conservative, so "once an untrusted issue body enters the context, the rest of the run is untrusted unless you explicitly drop it" (and the *drop* is where a bypass would live); approvals are coarse and don't expose the label algebra to the approving user; `quarantined_llm` is **single-turn and tools-free**, so multi-turn quarantined processing is unsupported. It is also **Python only** — .NET and Go agents get Agent Safety guidance and tool approval instead. AIRT should build test cases directly against this model: content that acquires a `trusted` label it shouldn't (a tool that returns third-party data without `source_integrity`), a sink reachable in untrusted context because it was never annotated, an exfiltration path through a sink whose cap is `user_identity`, label-laundering through a transformation tool, and injection delivered through `quarantined_llm` output — which is labeled untrusted but is still text the main model reasons over. AISPM should inventory FIDES adoption per agent, extract the label declarations on sources and sinks, and flag the four false-assurance configurations above

findings.title: ChatGPT's browser extension now covers Edge, Brave, Opera and Vivaldi, and the cloud browser can collect website credentials on web and mobile
findings.description: Two extensions of the browser-control surface reported on 2026-08-07, both **August 25**. **The extension footprint quadrupled**: ChatGPT's browser extension now works in **Microsoft Edge, Brave, Opera and Vivaldi** alongside Chrome, installed through **Settings > Computer Use** in the desktop app (with a "More browsers" expansion for browsers not listed), selected per chat by `@`-mention against the specific browser profile where the extension was installed. All five support tab mentions and browser control; Opera lacks side chat. Domain policy is per-browser and user-managed: **Manage** next to a browser exposes an **allowlist** of domains ChatGPT may use without asking again and a **blocklist** of domains it shouldn't touch. The coverage consequence is concrete: any ENDPOINT collector that detects ChatGPT browser control by looking for the Chrome extension ID, or that enumerates one browser's extension inventory, now under-reports on four additional browsers — and it under-reports on the **profile** dimension too, since the grant is per-browser-profile and the same machine can hold several. The **per-browser allowlist/blocklist is also new inventory**: it is the closest thing to a domain policy on this surface, it is set by the user rather than an admin, and its contents (particularly a broad allowlist) are a posture attribute worth reading. **The cloud browser can now take website credentials.** On eligible plans, ChatGPT Work on **web, iOS and Android** can prompt the user to "sign in to a supported website through the cloud browser," with **login details entered inside the sign-in flow rather than in chat** — an explicit design choice to keep credentials out of the conversation, which also means the authentication event does not appear in the transcript. Cloud browser sessions are documented as **isolated from local browsers**, so the resulting authenticated session lives entirely in OpenAI-hosted infrastructure: a durable, agent-usable session against a third-party site that exists on no endpoint Zenity can inspect and in no local browser profile. Both features are **excluded from Enterprise and Education workspaces**, which is the same asymmetry as the site-tools finding — the capability lands on the least-managed tiers. ENDPOINT should enumerate the ChatGPT extension across all five browsers and all profiles, read the per-browser allowlist/blocklist as policy state, and treat cloud-browser website sign-in as an off-endpoint session grant that must be inventoried from the ChatGPT side because it is invisible locally. AIDR should treat a cloud-browser authentication event as a distinct activity type from a local browser-control session. Sources: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/chrome-extension and https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/browser

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise added eight data stores and gave existing connectors write actions, including Supabase `execute SQL`, `apply migration` and `deploy edge function`
findings.description: Google's Gemini Enterprise connector surface grew twice in five days. **August 21 added seven data stores in Public Preview** — **Atlan** (data catalog/governance metadata), **Bitly**, **FactSet AI-Ready Data** (licensed financial data), **FullStory** (session replay and product analytics, i.e. recorded user behaviour), **Globalping**, **Pendo** and **Stripe** (payments) — each searchable and readable with natural language. **August 24 added the D&B Commercial Graph data store in Preview**, for searching and importing company data. Each is a new grounding source and therefore a new inventory entity, and the mix matters: FullStory and Stripe reach behavioural and payment data respectively, Atlan reaches the metadata that describes where everything else lives, and FactSet and D&B carry licensing obligations that make onward flow a compliance question, not just a security one. **But the sharper part of this release is the action expansion, because the actions are not reads.** Existing connectors gained: **Supabase — apply migration, deploy edge function, execute SQL, pause project, restore project**; **Descript — import media, prompt project agent, publish project**; **Gamma — generate Gamma**. The Supabase set alone is a database and serverless-platform control plane: `execute SQL` is arbitrary query execution, `apply migration` is schema change, `deploy edge function` is **code deployment**, and `pause project` / `restore project` are availability operations. A Gemini Enterprise agent holding these actions is not grounding on Supabase, it is **operating** Supabase — and `deploy edge function` in particular means an agent steered by untrusted grounding content can put attacker-influenced code into a running environment. `Descript — publish project` is likewise an external-publication sink. This is the pattern reported for custom MCP data stores on 2026-08-09 arriving through the first-party connector catalogue instead: the connector inventory can no longer be read as a list of data sources, because some entries are action grants with side effects. AISPM should inventory each new data store as a grounding source with its own sensitivity and licensing attributes, and — more importantly — should classify connector **actions** by effect rather than treating "connector attached" as one fact: separate read actions from write/deploy/destructive actions, flag any agent holding `execute SQL`, `apply migration` or `deploy edge function`, and treat the combination of an untrusted-content grounding source plus a write-capable connector action on the same agent as a toxic combination. Note the documented deployment constraint that helps here: Google recommends associating only one data store with actions belonging to a single connector type per app, and the Supabase data store is supported only in the `global`, `us` and `eu` locations. Sources: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/supabase and https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/introduction-to-connectors-and-data-stores

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise data-connector telemetry now identifies which connector tool an agent invoked and how long it took — an ingestion opportunity with a six-week retention cliff
findings.description: On **August 24** Google extended Cloud Monitoring telemetry for Gemini Enterprise data connectors in two ways. The existing count metric **`discoveryengine.googleapis.com/dataconnector/request_count`** gained three dimensions on top of its existing `status`: **`tool_id`** — "the identifier of the connector tool invoked" — **`engine_id`**, the Gemini Enterprise app identifier, and **`response_code`**, the gRPC response status. And a **new metric, `discoveryengine.googleapis.com/dataconnector/request_latencies` (Beta)**, reports "the distribution of tool invocation latency" in milliseconds with dimensions `status`, `response_code`, `tool_id` and `engine_id`. **The `tool_id` dimension is the part that changes what Zenity can see.** Until now this metric answered "how many connector requests, and did they succeed"; it now answers "**which connector tool, in which app, with what result**" — which is per-tool invocation attribution on a platform where the previous best signal was the `execute_tool` / `invoke_connector` trace spans reported on 2026-08-09. Paired with the previous finding, this is the detection layer for exactly the risk that finding describes: a Supabase `execute SQL` or `deploy edge function` invocation is now distinguishable by `tool_id` from a benign read, and attributable to a specific `engine_id`. AIDR should ingest both metrics, key on `tool_id` to build per-tool invocation baselines per app, and use `response_code` and the latency distribution as anomaly inputs — an unusual `tool_id` appearing under an `engine_id` that has never invoked it, a spike in denied `response_code`s (reconnaissance), or a latency profile shift on a write action are all detectable here and nowhere else on this platform. **Two caveats must ship with the ingestion.** These are **metrics, not logs** — they carry dimensions, counts and distributions, not arguments, results or the identity of the invoking user, so they establish *that* a named tool was invoked under an app, never *what* it did or *for whom*; correlating to a principal still requires the audit-log and trace surfaces. And retention is short: Gemini Enterprise metrics publish under the **`discoveryengine.googleapis.com/`** prefix, which falls in Google's "all other Google Cloud metrics" tier and is **retained six weeks by default** — so any investigation reaching back further than ~42 days finds nothing unless Zenity or the customer has already exported it. `request_latencies` is **Beta**, so its dimension set may still change

platforms.name: Kiro — first scan; three findings
details: **Powers — Kiro's implementation of the Agent Plugins standard.** A power is "a dynamic plugin that bundles specialized knowledge, tools, and workflows," structured as `plugin.json` (required manifest, declares **activation keywords**), `skills/`, an optional **`mcp.json`**, and an optional `dev.kiro/` for Kiro-specific steering extensions. Three install paths: the curated marketplace at `kiro.dev/powers` (partners include **Datadog, Figma, Stripe**) via one-click "Add to Kiro"; **any public GitHub repository URL**, where "a single repository can contain multiple powers, each in its own directory"; and a local folder for private repos. Activation is dynamic — Kiro "reads the task description, evaluates installed powers against the task, and loads only relevant powers into context" — rather than loading everything at startup. Kiro's own guidance is the only stated control: "Kiro powers are third-party tools that may be subject to separate terms. Only install powers from trusted sources." Source: https://kiro.dev/docs/powers/installation/

**`AGENTS.md` as always-on steering, discovered throughout the workspace tree** (IDE 1.0.309, Aug 13; CLI 2.18.0, Aug 12). Steering files live in `.kiro/steering/` (workspace) and `~/.kiro/steering/` (global, applies to *all* workspaces), with workspace winning on conflict. `AGENTS.md` is handled differently: it "**do[es] not support inclusion modes and [is] always included**," and Kiro "automatically discovers them in subdirectories throughout your workspace." Source: https://kiro.dev/docs/steering/

*(Held below the bar: CLI 2.19.0 (Aug 19) automatic stream recovery with an idle watchdog; IDE 1.0.337 (Aug 18) improved filesystem and command permission rules plus configured-terminal-profile execution on Windows; IDE 1.0.293 (Aug 11) Cloud Sessions for Agent Focus Mode; IDE 1.0.242 (Jul 28) guided hook-creation form. Confirmed from the 08-23 memo and still true: custom agents carry per-agent `mcpServers`/`tools`/`toolAliases` grants, MCP config exists at workspace and user scope, and both hot-reload from disk.)*

platforms.name: Cross-vendor — Agent Plugins 1.0.0 (August 6, 2026)
details: **An open, vendor-neutral specification for packaging agent extensions**, at `agent-plugins.org`, with the spec, JSON Schemas, governance and contribution process in a public GitHub repository (`agentplugins/agent-plugins-spec`). Version **1.0.0** is current; **1.1.0 is a working draft**. The Technical Steering Committee is drawn from **AWS, Cursor, Microsoft, OpenAI and Vercel** — "no single company's product roadmap sets the format's direction." Version 1.0.0 standardizes two component types: **Agent Skills** (reusable instructions and resources, each a folder with a `SKILL.md` carrying `name` and `description` frontmatter) and **MCP servers** (`mcp.json` describing **stdio, Streamable HTTP, or legacy HTTP+SSE** servers). The manifest's minimum is two fields — `$schema` and `name`. Clients discover components by scanning the directory structure; the spec **deliberately leaves installation, surfacing and distribution to each client**. Supported today by **ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Kiro and VS Code**. Sources: https://agent-plugins.org and https://vercel.com/blog/introducing-agent-plugins

**Agent Toolkit for AWS** — official AWS-supported MCP servers, skills and plugins, bundling **30+ curated skills** across service selection, CDK/CloudFormation, serverless (Lambda), containers, storage (S3, DynamoDB), IAM policy configuration, observability, billing, SDK usage and deployment, plus skills for **building agents on Bedrock and AgentCore** and for **data-lake/analytics/ETL work with S3 Tables, Glue and Athena**. Four install paths, including runtime retrieval through the AWS MCP Server with no local installation. Plugins ship for **Claude Code, Codex and Cursor**; Kiro consumes the same content as Powers. platforms.name: Google Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform — Agent Identity (coverage-gap recovery)
details: **Agent Identity — a SPIFFE-based, per-agent cryptographic identity that is a first-class IAM principal.** Format: `spiffe://TRUST_DOMAIN/resources/SERVICE/RESOURCE_PATH`, e.g. `spiffe://agents.global.org-123456789012.system.id.goog/resources/aiplatform/projects/9876543210/locations/us-central1/reasoningEngines/my-test-agent`; in IAM policy the same identity appears with a **`principal://`** prefix. On deployment, "Google Cloud assigns it a unique SPIFFE identity and an X.509 certificate," **auto-renewed every 24 hours**. Explicitly contrasted with service accounts: agent identities "are not shared by multiple workloads by default, can't be impersonated, and don't allow developers to generate long-lived service account keys." Agents authenticate to **MCP servers, cloud resources, other agents and external tools**, either on their own authority (bound access tokens for Google Cloud; 2-legged OAuth, API keys or HTTP basic for external services) or **on behalf of an end user via 3-legged OAuth**. Governance surfaces: IAM allow **and deny** policies, **Principal Access Boundary (PAB)**, VPC Service Controls, and default **Context-Aware Access policies enforcing mTLS and DPoP token binding**. Audit logs distinguish "when the agent is acting as itself and when it is acting on behalf of an end user." Administrator visibility of the SPIFFE ID on the Agent details page is **Public Preview**, with the Agent Registry resource ID as fallback. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/agent-identity-overview

findings.title: Agent Plugins 1.0 — one open, vendor-neutral bundle format carrying skills *and* MCP server configuration, already live in ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Kiro and VS Code
findings.description: On **August 6, 2026** AWS, Cursor, Microsoft, OpenAI and Vercel published **Agent Plugins 1.0.0** as an openly-licensed specification with a shared Technical Steering Committee, at `agent-plugins.org`, with schemas and governance in a public repo. A plugin is a directory: a **`plugin.json`** manifest (minimum two fields — `$schema` and `name` — plus, in practice, activation keywords), an optional **`skills/`** folder of `SKILL.md` files in the Agent Skills format, and an optional **`mcp.json`** describing **stdio, Streamable HTTP or legacy HTTP+SSE** MCP servers. **This monitor has been reporting the same thing under several vendor names, and that framing is now wrong.** On 2026-08-07 it reported "Codex Agent Plugins" as an OpenAI capability with an OpenAI-specific marketplace path; on 2026-08-23 it reported Foundry's Skills API and the `agentskills.io` specification; Kiro's Powers, the Agent Toolkit for AWS, and Vercel's implementation are the same format again. The single most important consequence is that **an extension artifact is now portable across six clients from five vendors**, so per-vendor extension inventory cannot establish what an endpoint is running — a plugin authored once, installed from one marketplace, appears in a developer's Codex session, their Cursor session, their VS Code/GitHub Copilot session and their Kiro session, and each vendor's own management surface sees only its own slice. **The second consequence is that the bundle is a tool-and-connection grant, not documentation.** Because `mcp.json` travels inside the plugin, installing a plugin installs MCP servers — and the spec **deliberately leaves installation, surfacing and distribution to each client** ("preserving their ability to differentiate"), which means there is no standard trust prompt, no standard provenance record and no standard enablement gate; each client invents its own, and one of them (see the next finding) does not write installed servers to its own config file at all. **Third: the spec has no security-considerations section.** Neither `agent-plugins.org`, the AWS announcement, the Vercel announcement, nor the spec repo contains one — so the format that now moves instruction content and MCP connections between six agent clients ships with no normative guidance on trust, signing, or provenance. **1.1.0 is already a working draft**, so the component set will grow, and a new component type will change the surface on six clients at once. ENDPOINT should model "Agent Plugin" as a **cross-vendor entity type with one identity and many install sites** rather than as N per-vendor features: enumerate plugin directories on developer machines, parse `plugin.json` for identity and `mcp.json` for the servers and transports each grants, resolve the origin (marketplace, git remote, local path) as provenance, and reconcile the same plugin observed across different clients as one artifact. AISPM should treat a plugin's `skills/` bodies as privilege-shaping instruction content and its `mcp.json` as a connection inventory, and should expect the vendor-side registries to be incomplete by design. AIRT should treat a plugin as a single vector that reaches every compliant client at once. Sources: https://agent-plugins.org and https://vercel.com/blog/introducing-agent-plugins

findings.title: Kiro installs plugin-format MCP servers *without* writing them to `~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json` — the canonical MCP config file is no longer a complete inventory
findings.description: Kiro's implementation of Agent Plugins is called **Powers**, and its installation documentation draws a distinction that breaks endpoint MCP discovery: for **Agent Plugins (`plugin.json`) format**, "**MCP servers are managed internally by Kiro and are not added to your user-level `~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json` file**," whereas for the **legacy `POWER.md` format**, "servers register in the `~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json` configuration file under the Powers section." So the same capability — an MCP server reachable by the agent — is visible in the config file or invisible in it **depending purely on which packaging format the power used**, and the newer, standard, marketplace-endorsed format is the invisible one. Any collector that enumerates MCP servers by reading `mcp.json` (the obvious and previously correct approach, and the one the 2026-08-23 memo recorded for Kiro) now systematically under-reports, and it under-reports in the direction of the format the whole industry is converging on. Three further specifics make this actionable. **The install surface is wide open**: powers install from the curated marketplace at `kiro.dev/powers` (Datadog, Figma and Stripe among the partners) with one click, **from any public GitHub repository URL** — where "a single repository can contain multiple powers, each in its own directory," so one URL can carry several tool grants — or from a local folder for private repos. **Activation is dynamic and content-driven**: Kiro "reads the task description, evaluates installed powers against the task, and loads only relevant powers into context," with activation keywords declared in `plugin.json`. That means *installed* and *active* are different sets, the active set changes per prompt, and which tools an agent holds at a given moment is a function of text the user typed — so point-in-time capability inventory is wrong for the same reason hot-reloading MCP config is, and the two compound. **The only documented control is advice**: "Kiro powers are third-party tools that may be subject to separate terms. Only install powers from trusted sources." No trust prompt, no signing, no approval workflow is documented. Urgency is inherited, not speculative: AWS is pushing the entire Amazon Q Developer IDE plugin population onto Kiro by **April 30, 2027**. ENDPOINT must enumerate Kiro powers from Kiro's own power storage rather than from `mcp.json`, parse each power's `mcp.json` for the servers and transports it grants, record install provenance (marketplace entry, GitHub URL, or local path) per power, treat the `plugin.json` activation keywords as the mapping from prompt text to tool availability, and continue to read `.kiro/agents` and both MCP config scopes for the hot-reload surface — while flagging that `mcp.json` alone is now an incomplete answer

findings.title: Google Cloud Agent Identity — a SPIFFE-based per-agent identity that appears in IAM policy as a new `principal://` principal type
findings.description: Google has shipped a distinct identity primitive for agents, and it is not a service account. Every agent deployed on Google Cloud receives "a strongly attested, cryptographic identity … based on the SPIFFE standard," formatted `spiffe://TRUST_DOMAIN/resources/SERVICE/RESOURCE_PATH` — e.g. `spiffe://agents.global.org-123456789012.system.id.goog/resources/aiplatform/projects/9876543210/locations/us-central1/reasoningEngines/my-test-agent` — together with an **auto-provisioned X.509 certificate that renews every 24 hours**. In IAM policy the identity is bound with a **`principal://` prefix**, and that detail is the first concrete action item: **any IAM policy parser that recognizes `serviceAccount:`, `user:`, `group:` and `domain:` members but not `principal://` will silently fail to attribute agent grants**, reading a policy as having no agent bindings when it has several. Google states the security properties as deliberate contrasts with service accounts — agent identities "are not shared by multiple workloads by default, can't be impersonated, and don't allow developers to generate long-lived service account keys" — which inverts the usual posture question: the finding is no longer "which agents share a service account and who can mint keys for it," but **"which agents still run on a service account instead of an agent identity,"** and that becomes a discoverable, alertable posture gap. The reach is broad and squarely in AISPM's remit: an agent identity authenticates to **MCP servers, cloud resources, other agents, and external tools and services**, either **on its own authority** (bound access tokens for Google Cloud; 2-legged OAuth, API keys or HTTP basic auth externally) or **on behalf of an end user via 3-legged OAuth** — so the same agent principal holds two materially different privilege envelopes, one bounded by the user's consent and one bounded only by the agent's own IAM, and the audit logs distinguish them ("clear audit logs both when the agent is acting as itself and when it is acting on behalf of an end user"). That distinction is the single highest-value signal here and AIDR should key on it: an agent operating under its own authority on data it only ever reached on a user's behalf is a privilege-escalation pattern that is visible in these logs and nowhere else. The governance surfaces are also new inventory: IAM **allow and deny** policies on agent principals, **Principal Access Boundary (PAB)** restricting which resources an agent may touch at all, VPC Service Controls, and **default Context-Aware Access policies enforcing mTLS and DPoP token binding** — a default that is worth reading as a baseline, because an agent whose CAA policy has been relaxed away from mTLS/DPoP is a downgrade Zenity can detect. Administrator visibility of the SPIFFE ID on the Gemini Enterprise Agent details page is **Public Preview**, and when a publisher does not publish a SPIFFE ID the console shows the **Agent Registry resource ID as a fallback** — so the console cannot be trusted as a uniform source of agent identity, and the presence of a fallback ID is itself a signal that an agent is running without an attested identity. **Note the mis-mapping hazard that caused this to be missed**: this monitor reported "Agent Identity" on 2026-08-10, but that was Microsoft's **Entra Agent ID**. The two are unrelated implementations of the same idea, and Zenity should model "attested per-agent identity" once with per-vendor bindings — Entra Agent ID, Google SPIFFE agent identity, and AgentCore's workload access tokens — rather than three unrelated features. AISPM should discover agent identities per project, parse `principal://` members out of IAM allow and deny policies, inventory PAB bindings and CAA policies per agent identity, flag agents still bound to service accounts, and flag any agent whose identity resolves only to a registry resource ID

findings.title: Kiro loads `AGENTS.md` from every subdirectory of a workspace, always, with no inclusion mode and no trust gate
findings.description: Kiro **IDE 1.0.309 (Aug 13)** and **CLI 2.18.0 (Aug 12)** added support for `AGENTS.md` as steering context "from anywhere in your workspace tree," and the steering documentation states the two properties whose combination is the finding: `AGENTS.md` files "**do not support inclusion modes and are always included**," and Kiro "**automatically discovers them in subdirectories throughout your workspace**." Contrast this with Kiro's own steering files, which live in `.kiro/steering/` and carry an explicit inclusion mode in YAML front matter — `always`, `fileMatch` (loaded only when working on matching files), `manual` (loaded only when referenced as `#steering-file-name`), or `auto` (loaded when the request matches the description). Those modes are a real, if coarse, scoping control, and `AGENTS.md` has none of them: a file placed in any directory of any repository the developer opens is unconditionally injected into the agent's context. Three properties make this a genuine injection vector rather than a configuration footnote. **It is repository-sourced**, so a dependency vendored into a subdirectory, a monorepo package owned by another team, or a cloned third-party project all carry instruction text that loads with no review — the same failure mode as Anthropic's repository-mounted skills (reported 2026-08-09), but with the scoping control removed rather than merely coarse. **`AGENTS.md` is a cross-vendor filename**, adopted well beyond Kiro, so a single file authored to steer one agent is read by whichever compliant agent opens the tree — the author of the file and the operator of the agent reading it need have no relationship. **And global steering compounds it**: `~/.kiro/steering/` "applies to all workspaces," so instruction content can be positioned once at user scope and reach every project the developer subsequently opens, with workspace files overriding on conflict. No trust prompt or approval mechanism for steering content is documented anywhere in the steering docs. AIRT should test whether instructions in a nested `AGENTS.md` — introduced through a dependency directory or a subrepo rather than the project root — steer tool selection, alter which powers activate, or suppress the agent's own safety behaviour, and should treat the nesting depth as part of the test because discovery is recursive. ENDPOINT should inventory every `AGENTS.md` in an open workspace tree plus the global `~/.kiro/steering/` directory, record content hashes and the git provenance of each file (authored locally, or arrived via a dependency or clone), and treat an `AGENTS.md` that appears in a directory the developer does not own as a distinct posture condition

findings.title: Agent Toolkit for AWS — 30+ AWS-authored skills plus official MCP servers, reaching four agent clients, with one install path that leaves nothing on disk
findings.description: AWS publishes an official first-party bundle of "MCP servers, skills, and plugins to help AI agents build on AWS," carrying **30+ curated skills** across service selection, **CDK/CloudFormation**, serverless (**Lambda**), containers, storage (**S3, DynamoDB**), **IAM policy configuration**, observability, billing, SDK usage and deployment — plus dedicated skill sets for **building agents on Bedrock and AgentCore** and for **data-lake/analytics/ETL work with S3 Tables, Glue and Athena**. Plugins ship today for **Claude Code, Codex and Cursor**; Kiro consumes the same content as Powers. Three things make this worth its own inventory line rather than a footnote to the Agent Plugins finding. **It is the concrete, high-privilege instance of the portable-bundle problem**: this is not a formatting utility but a package that equips an IDE agent to operate real AWS infrastructure — provisioning via CDK/CloudFormation, S3 and DynamoDB access, Lambda deployment, IAM policy authoring, billing data — and it reaches four different agent clients from one authoring source, so the same AWS-operating capability can arrive on a developer machine through whichever client that developer happens to use. **There are four install paths and one of them leaves nothing on disk.** Skills arrive bundled with a plugin; downloaded individually from the GitHub repo into the agent's skills directory; through an AWS CLI wizard (`aws configure agent-toolkit`) that "**detects supported agents on your system and installs skills into each agent's configuration directory**" — one command that fans a single grant out to every agent client on the machine; or **discovered at runtime through the AWS MCP Server "without any local installation,"** where the agent calls `search_documentation` to find a skill and `retrieve_skill` to load it into context. That last path is the one that matters most for coverage: **an agent can acquire and act on AWS-operating instructions with no on-disk artifact to inventory at all**, so file-based endpoint collection cannot see it and only MCP-call telemetry can — `retrieve_skill` is therefore a named activity type AIDR should record, not just a tool call. **And skills load on demand and are then released** ("after the task is complete, your agent releases the skill content from context"), so installed, loaded and active are three different sets and the agent's effective AWS capability at any moment is not a static property. The privilege that matters is not the skill text but the credential the agent already holds: instruction content that competently drives CDK, IAM and Lambda turns an ambiently-available AWS credential on a developer laptop into an infrastructure-change path — exactly the toxic combination of broad local credentials plus capable tooling that AISPM exists to flag. AISPM should treat the Agent Toolkit as a named, discoverable installed component per endpoint, resolve which of its plugins/skills are present and which client hosts them, and correlate its presence against the AWS credentials and assumed roles available on that machine — an endpoint with the toolkit installed and a long-lived administrative AWS credential is a materially different posture than one with either alone. ENDPOINT should record the toolkit's MCP servers alongside the plugin-format caveat in the Kiro finding above, since on Kiro these servers will not appear in `~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json`

platforms.name: Microsoft Foundry — no new release content; one never-read API surface
details: **The Foundry Skills API (`{endpoint}/skills`) — preview.** A skill is a `SKILL.md` file following the [agentskills.io](https://agentskills.io) specification (YAML front matter `name` + `description`, Markdown body that "becomes the skill's injected instructions"), stored centrally through a **versioned API**. Creating a version auto-creates the parent skill; **every update creates a new immutable `SkillVersion`**, and the parent `Skill` tracks `default_version` and `latest_version`. Full CRUD plus content download as a ZIP: `POST|GET|DELETE {endpoint}/skills[/{name}[/versions[/{v}]]]`, `GET .../content`. All calls require the **`Foundry-Features: Skills=V1Preview`** header and a bearer token scoped `https://ai.azure.com/.default`; RBAC is **Foundry User** on the project. Two delivery modes: **attach to a toolbox**, where skills surface as **MCP Resources** under the SEP-2640 Skills extension so any client calling `resources/list`/`resources/read` — "GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, or your own agent harness … without any Foundry SDK" — discovers and loads them; or **download directly** into a hosted or local agent project for per-session context injection. The VS Code Toolkit ships a **prebuilt skill catalog** (`docx`, `pptx`, `xlsx`, `pdf`, `canvas-design`, `algorithmic-art`, `brand-guidelines`, `theme-factory`, `doc-coauthoring`, `internal-comms`, `slack-gif-creator`). Limitations worth recording: **the Skills API is not reachable over a private endpoint**, so a Foundry resource with public network access disabled cannot use skills at all; and `azd ai skill create --force` **deletes the existing skill and all of its versions** before uploading. Microsoft's own caution: "Customers are responsible for understanding the behaviors of any skills deployed and the data handling practices of any external endpoints receiving data." Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/tools/skills

findings.title: Claude Mythos 5 is Fable 5 with its cyber safeguards lifted, entitled per-organization through Anthropic, AWS *or* Google Cloud
findings.description: The watch item opened on 2026-08-21 resolves into the most consequential finding of this scan, and Anthropic states the core fact directly: Mythos 5 is "**the same model as Claude Fable 5 but with cyber safeguards lifted**." The mechanism is **classifier removal** — Fable 5 runs three real-time safety classifiers that route sensitive queries, and on Mythos 5 those classifiers are absent, which is precisely what permits unrestricted offensive security analysis for legitimate defensive work. Three consequences follow, and the first strikes at an assumption inside Zenity's own product. **Guardrail behaviour is a property of the deployment, not of the model.** Any AIRT baseline, any AIDR detection tuned to "what this model refuses," and any posture rule that infers safety posture from a model family is wrong for this tier — two entitlements to the *same weights* behave differently, and nothing but the model identifier `claude-mythos-5` distinguishes them. Refusal-based guardrail probes will silently report a pass on a model that has no guardrail to bypass. **Access is a gated, auditable, multi-cloud entitlement.** Mythos 5 "is offered only to approved customers in Project Glasswing," requires an Anthropic invitation, a **signed NDA**, and approval coordinated with the **US government** — and, critically for discovery, the documented request path is to "contact your **Anthropic, AWS, or Google Cloud account team**." So the entitlement can arrive through a hyperscaler relationship rather than a direct Anthropic contract, meaning an organization may hold classifier-free model access that never appears in its Anthropic tenant at all. Zenity must look for it on all three surfaces. The population is not hypothetical: Glasswing's launch partners are **AWS, Apple, Broadcom, Cisco, CrowdStrike, Google, JPMorganChase, the Linux Foundation, Microsoft, NVIDIA and Palo Alto Networks**, and the Mythos 5 rollout expanded the programme to roughly **150 organizations across more than 15 countries** — a meaningful share of large enterprises, several of them likely Zenity customers. **And it is the direct structural analogue of OpenAI's Daybreak Red / GPT-5.6-Cyber tier** reported 2026-08-14, where OpenAI's own evaluation showed **95%** compliance on advanced offensive prompts versus **1.5%** for the default-protected model. This is now a **cross-vendor pattern**, so Zenity should model "safeguard-lifted / cyber-capable model entitlement" once as an entity type and map it per vendor rather than treating each programme as bespoke. AIRT should build a distinct baseline for safeguard-lifted tiers and stop treating refusal as a signal on them. AISPM should discover which models an organization is actually entitled to across Anthropic, Bedrock and Vertex/Gemini, treat `claude-mythos-5` and the GPT-5.x-Cyber tiers as privileged entitlements requiring named ownership and written justification, and flag any agent, API key or workspace configured against one. Note the discovery hazard that caused this to be missed for months: **Mythos 5 appears in ordinary model-availability lists alongside Fable 5, Opus 5 and Sonnet 5**, so it reads as one more model rather than as a control-stripped tier

findings.title: AgentCore Memory now extracts non-conversational JSON — activity logs and system events become durable agent memory
findings.description: `CreateEvent` accepts a new **`json` payload type** carrying "non-conversational, JSON-formatted data—such as behavioral events, activity logs, or system events—**up to 100 KB for each payload**," and the API reference is explicit about the consequence: "**Conversational and JSON payloads are extracted into long-term memory. Blob payloads are stored in short-term memory only and are not extracted.**" JSON payloads run through the **semantic, user-preference, summarization and episodic** strategies. This is an extension of an existing API rather than a new service, but it changes the shape of the memory-poisoning problem in three specific ways. **The write path no longer requires a conversation.** Until now, durable agent memory grew from turns — something a user or an agent said. Now any system that can emit a `CreateEvent` writes memory directly, so the set of principals able to influence what an agent believes expands from conversational participants to every telemetry producer wired into the memory store — and the natural implementations here (activity logs, behavioural event streams, system events) are exactly the sources nobody classifies as attacker-influenceable. **It is machine-scale.** 100 KB per payload of structured data, streamed continuously, is a far higher-bandwidth channel into LLM-driven extraction than conversational turns, and extraction is the step where stored content becomes agent belief. **And the blob/JSON asymmetry is the detection rule.** A blob is inert — short-term only, never extracted; a JSON payload of the same bytes is extracted into long-term memory and will shape future sessions. So the payload *type* field is what determines whether stored data can influence the agent later, and it is the field a detection must key on rather than the payload size or source. AIDR should treat `CreateEvent` with a `json` payload as a distinct activity type from a conversational one, record the emitting principal rather than only the `actorId`, and monitor volume and provenance — a spike in JSON events from a non-conversational source is memory growth no human authored. AISPM should enumerate which memory stores accept JSON payloads, resolve which identities hold `CreateEvent` permission on each, and flag stores whose write population is broader than their conversational population; a memory store fed by system telemetry and shared across agents is a cross-agent influence channel. AIRT should test whether crafted values inside a JSON activity-log payload survive extraction into long-term memory and steer a later session

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry's Skills API is a versioned skill resource that any MCP client can load without a Foundry SDK
findings.description: Foundry stores skills centrally through a **versioned Skills API** at `{FOUNDRY_PROJECT_ENDPOINT}/skills`, gated behind the **`Foundry-Features: Skills=V1Preview`** header, with **Foundry User** RBAC on the project. A skill is a `SKILL.md` file following the agentskills.io specification whose Markdown body "becomes the skill's injected instructions." The versioning model is the useful half for posture: creating a version **auto-creates the parent skill**, **every update produces a new immutable `SkillVersion`**, and the parent `Skill` carries **`default_version`** and **`latest_version`** — so promoting a new default is a **metadata-only repoint that silently changes behaviour for every agent and toolbox referencing the skill unpinned**, and whether a given reference is pinned or floating is a discoverable, alertable property. The distribution model is what makes this more than a footnote to the toolbox finding reported 2026-08-09. Skills attached to a toolbox surface as **MCP Resources** under the **SEP-2640** Skills extension: a client calls `resources/list` once at startup and `resources/read` to pull content, and Microsoft states plainly that "**any MCP client — GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, or your own agent harness — can consume skills this way without any Foundry SDK**." So Foundry becomes a **skill distribution point for non-Microsoft agents**, and instruction text authored and governed inside a Foundry project executes inside clients Foundry has no visibility into — which also means the Foundry-side inventory is the *only* place that reach is enumerable. Two further specifics belong in coverage. **The Skills API has no private-endpoint support** — a Foundry resource with public network access disabled cannot create, manage or download skills at all — so adopting skills requires a network-posture concession that is itself worth flagging. And the VS Code Toolkit ships a **prebuilt catalog** (`docx`, `pptx`, `xlsx`, `pdf`, `canvas-design`, `algorithmic-art`, `brand-guidelines`, `theme-factory`, `doc-coauthoring`, `internal-comms`, `slack-gif-creator`) registerable into a project from a card, so third-party-authored instruction content enters the estate with no procurement step. Microsoft's own caution confirms where responsibility sits: customers must understand "the behaviors of any skills deployed and the data handling practices of any external endpoints receiving data." AISPM should enumerate skills and versions through `/skills`, record `default_version` versus `latest_version` and which references are pinned, read skill bodies as privilege-shaping instruction content, and reconcile Foundry-registered skills against skills observed loading in external MCP clients; AIRT should treat skill content as a persistent injection vector and specifically test whether a default-version promotion changes agent behaviour with no agent-side change. **Note: this is a coverage-gap recovery, not new platform movement** — the page carries `ms.date` 2026-08-05

findings.title: Devin Desktop shares terminal output and pre-commit edits with third-party ACP agent subprocesses
findings.description: Devin Desktop **v3.8.20 (Aug 21)** adds settings that "control whether **terminal and user-edit activity share with ACP agents**." What is new is the *control*, and the control is what makes the underlying flow legible — but the receiving side is the finding. **Agent Client Protocol is JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdin/stdout, and the editor launches the agent as a subprocess**, so an ACP agent is a local process with a live feed from the IDE. Devin Desktop supports **Codex, Claude Agent, OpenCode and any other ACP-compatible agent, "including agents built by your team in-house,"** and those third-party agents appear in the Kanban view **alongside** Devin, **share the Spaces context layer**, and "operate with the same controls as native sessions" — i.e. they are peers of the first-party agent, not sandboxed guests. Two data classes are therefore leaving the endpoint to a party the vendor does not operate. **Terminal output** is among the highest-value content on a developer machine: it routinely carries environment variables, connection strings, tokens echoed by CLI tools, and the contents of failed authentication attempts. **User-edit activity** is a live stream of proprietary source *before* it reaches version control, so it bypasses every control anchored to the SCM. Because ACP is an open protocol and in-house agents are explicitly supported, the destination is not enumerable from the vendor's surface — the setting's state on a given machine is the only local evidence that the flow is active, which makes it a required collection target rather than a nice-to-have. Two adjacent v3.8.20 items sharpen the scope picture: **workspace trust prompts now appear when needed to activate local agents**, confirming that local agent activation is gated on a per-workspace trust decision a developer makes unilaterally and that Zenity can read as a posture signal; and **multi-root workspaces with virtual filesystem folders** widen what one agent session can see, since a virtual root can compose directories that no single project boundary contains. Reported despite Windsurf's watching tier because this is an endpoint egress channel, not an agent convenience. ENDPOINT should detect the ACP sharing setting's state per install, enumerate attached ACP agents and resolve who operates each, treat enabled terminal-sharing on a machine holding production credentials as a high-risk condition, and inventory per-workspace trust decisions and multi-root workspace composition as agent scope attributes

findings.title: OpenAI's official Python SDK now supports the Bedrock Runtime endpoint — the cross-provider observability break is no longer confined to Codex CLI
findings.description: `openai-python` **v3.2.0 (Aug 17)** adds "**Bedrock Runtime endpoint support (SDK-290)**." On 2026-08-21 this monitor reported the same capability arriving in **Codex CLI 0.148.0** and framed it as a coding-agent quirk that compounded two known blind spots. Its arrival in the **SDK** changes the scope of that finding materially: it is no longer a property of one client that developers choose to install, but of **the library any application uses to call OpenAI**, so cross-provider routing is now available to arbitrary production workloads rather than to interactive coding sessions. The compounding facts are unchanged and worth restating because they now apply far more broadly. Anthropic's Compliance API — the richest available source of local Claude Code and Cowork transcripts — **explicitly does not capture sessions routed through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud or Microsoft Foundry**. And as of 2026-08-21, `bedrock-runtime` **serves the Anthropic Messages API on its `/anthropic` route and the OpenAI shapes on `/openai/v1`**. So an application built on the OpenAI SDK, pointed at Bedrock Runtime, running a Claude model, produces traffic that OpenAI does not see, that Anthropic's compliance surface does not capture, and that arrives at AWS in a wire format whose parser selection Zenity is only now correcting to key on route path rather than hostname. The general rule this reinforces: **per-vendor telemetry cannot establish coverage once the vendors' own SDKs route to each other's endpoints — the only reliable vantage point is the cloud account's own logging.** Two smaller items in the same release stream belong in schema work rather than as separate findings: v3.2.0 also adds "**shell call streaming events** and new service/image types," which implies a command-execution surface reflected in the streaming schema, and v3.1.0 (Aug 14) adds a "**workload identity access token issued event**." AIDR should stop treating OpenAI-shaped traffic as OpenAI-destined, ensure AWS-side logging covers Bedrock traffic originating from OpenAI SDK clients, and add the new streaming event types to its parsers; AISPM should discover OpenAI SDK base-URL and endpoint configuration as a posture attribute, since the endpoint an application targets is a configuration choice invisible from the credential alone

findings.title: Salesforce Winter '27's Marketing Goals Agent holds a budget and optimizes autonomously, and the second marketing agent is now named
findings.description: Two upgrades to the caveated finding carried on 2026-08-21. The second Winter '27 marketing agent is **Agentforce Content Agent**, which creates campaign content at scale while maintaining brand consistency — so the pair is now fully named rather than half-named. More importantly, the **Marketing Goals Agent's autonomy model is now documented**, and it is stronger than last scan's "translates objectives into strategies": users "define a goal, **budget**, and eligible audience," the agent proposes a strategy for human review and approval, and then — once activated — "**operates autonomously within those guardrails, continuously optimizing** activities and decisions toward the desired outcome." That is a standing grant, not a task: a human approves once, and the agent thereafter makes ongoing spend and targeting decisions with no per-decision review. Three things follow. The **budget is a governance object**, and it is the same pattern as the AgentCore session budget reported 2026-08-21 — the ceiling a human sets is the only real bound on autonomous commercial action, which makes budget configuration a posture attribute of the first order rather than an operational setting, and makes a large or absent budget a finding in itself. The **approval boundary is one-time**, so "was this reviewed?" has a materially different answer than for a conversational agent; Zenity should record the activation event and its approver as the authorization for everything the agent subsequently does. And the **eligible audience is a standing data-scope grant** — a marketing agent optimizing against an audience is reading and acting on prospect and campaign data continuously, not per-request. Also confirmed this scan: **Agentforce observability** ships with refined agent analytics and **custom scorers**, some in Beta, alongside agent interoperability, improved voice and multilingual support. **The caveat from last scan stands and must be honoured**: every specific here is **WebSearch-corroborated only**. `www.salesforce.com/releases/` is still 403, the JS-rendered `help.salesforce.com` release-notes viewer still cannot be read by WebFetch, and while `agentforce/guide` recovered from its 503 it is release-agnostic and confirms nothing about Winter '27. AISPM should add both prebuilt agents to the Agentforce inventory once vendor-confirmed, treat the Marketing Goals Agent's budget and eligible audience as first-class inventory attributes with the activation approver recorded, and match on stable identifiers rather than display names given the concurrent Lead Nurturing→Engagement rename

findings.title: AWS is migrating the entire Amazon Q Developer IDE population to Kiro, an agentic IDE with per-agent MCP grants that this monitor has never scanned
findings.description: AWS will **discontinue support for Amazon Q Developer IDE plugins on April 30, 2027** and directs users to **Kiro**, stating that "everything you rely on today (inline suggestions, chat, and code generation) is available in Kiro," which adds "agentic coding, chat and MCP support." The end-of-support notice itself is a deprecation and not reportable; the **named migration target is**, and Kiro's own documentation shows a surface squarely inside ENDPOINT's remit. Kiro runs "**one unified agent harness that powers every surface (IDE, CLI, Web, and Mobile)**," so a single configuration follows the developer across four form factors rather than being scoped to an editor. It supports **custom agents** whose configuration files carry an **`mcpServers` field specifying which MCP servers that agent may reach**, plus a `tools` field selecting individual tools from each source and `toolAliases` for naming conflicts — meaning per-agent tool grants are declarative, file-based, and enumerable, which is good news for discovery and bad news if nobody is reading them. MCP config exists at **both workspace and user scope** (`Kiro: Open workspace MCP config` / `Open user MCP config`), and both **hot-reload from disk** via a file watcher on `.kiro/agents` directories and `mcp.json` — so an agent's capability set can change mid-session with no restart and no UI event, which defeats point-in-time capability inventory in exactly the way Anthropic's repository-mounted skills did (reported 2026-08-09). The urgency is that this is an **inherited installed base, not organic adoption**: AWS is actively pushing a population off Q Developer plugins onto Kiro by a known date. There are now **two** named Amazon successors absent from `sources.json` — **Amazon Quick** (flagged 2026-08-21) and **Kiro** — while primary-tier polling budget is spent weekly confirming that Amazon Q is still dead (Q Business closed to new customers 2026-07-31; its newest feature entry remains **Agentic RAG, August 14, 2025**; Q Developer's doc history has not moved in ~3 months). ENDPOINT should stand up Kiro detection now rather than after the migration: inventory `.kiro/agents` definitions and both MCP config scopes, resolve per-agent `mcpServers` and `tools` grants, treat hot-reload as a continuous-change surface requiring re-enumeration rather than one-time collection, and model the four surfaces (IDE, CLI, Web, Mobile) as one identity with one configuration. This scan **recommends adding `kiro.dev/docs` and its changelog to `sources.json` and demoting Amazon Q from primary-tier polling** — the second consecutive scan making that recommendation
